## The problem

Our team of twelve engineers is now spending more time managing merges than shipping features. Feature branches routinely live for two to four weeks, and by the time they're ready to merge, they've drifted so far from main that integration becomes a multi-day ordeal of conflict resolution and re-testing. Two outcomes follow directly from this: releases slip because "integration week" is unpredictable, and bugs surface only after several branches collide, making them far harder to trace to a single cause. We are optimizing for isolated convenience while paying a hidden, compounding integration tax.

## The proposal

I propose we adopt trunk-based development: everyone commits to main at least daily, incomplete work ships behind feature flags, and we invest in a CI pipeline fast and reliable enough to gate every commit.

- Merge to main at least once per day, in small, reviewable increments
- Gate unfinished features with flags rather than isolating them on branches
- Require CI (build, unit tests, lint) to pass before merge, with a target pipeline time under ten minutes
- Use short-lived branches (hours, not weeks) only for the commit-to-review window
- Run a two-week pilot with one squad before rolling out team-wide

This shrinks the blast radius of every change, surfaces conflicts while context is still fresh, and lets us decouple "deployed" from "released" via flags.

## What could go wrong

The strongest objection is real: without discipline, trunk-based development can turn main into a perpetually half-broken branch, especially for a team of twelve where not everyone is equally rigorous about test coverage or flag hygiene. If CI is slow or flaky, "commit daily" becomes "commit and hope," and we could end up worse off than with long-lived branches, where at least main stays stable. I take this seriously — it means the CI investment isn't optional, it's the precondition. We should not flip the switch team-wide until pipeline reliability and speed are proven in the pilot.

Other risks are more manageable: flag sprawl can be controlled with a flag-cleanup policy, and reviewers will need to adjust to smaller, more frequent pull requests rather than sprawling ones.

I would like a decision by the end of next week.
